original_statement:
In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust workspace that adopts Aspergillus gets every ASP rule checked mechanically on commit, the same way Python and TypeScript consumers do, including two whole-workspace checks: the same function body defined twice, and the same concept declared as a type in more than one crate.
Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus (first consumer: lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates), and the exophial workers committing into them.
How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. A consumer copies or depends on aspergillus/rust (as it does today for rust/configs/clippy.toml) and runs the Rust rules over its workspace; each finding prints as `path:line: ASPnnn` and a finding in a blocking rule fails the run. docs/design.md's Rust column names, for every rule of Levels 2 and 3 and every ASP4xx rule that applies to Rust, the enforcing check: a clippy lint, a declarative ast-grep YAML rule under rust/ast-grep-rules/ (the engine TypeScript already uses under typescript/ast-grep-rules/), or a whole-workspace check; a rule the Rust language already enforces names the language feature, and a rule that does not apply to Rust says why. No entry reads 'Manual', 'planned' or 'Module structure'. A duplicate-function check reports two Rust functions whose normalized bodies are identical, as `aspergillus check-duplicates` does for Python. A duplicate-type check reports a struct or enum declared in one crate whose concept a type in another crate of the same workspace already declares, with an allowlist for intended cases.
What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. Run against lobaria integrated a027fb9, the duplicate-type check reports the three declarations of Nanos (statechart/src/units.rs, pump-strategy/src/units.rs, hold-time-curve/src/input.rs) and of Receipt (statechart/src/edge.rs, pump-strategy/src/units.rs, hold-time-curve/src/input.rs) as findings. The ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 and ASP206 Rust checks each report a finding on a committed Rust fixture that violates the rule and none on a committed fixture that satisfies it, for every rule that has a Rust check. docs/design.md's Rust column has no 'Manual', 'planned' or 'Module structure' entry. A Rust consumer runs the checks with cargo and the ast-grep crates (ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config, ast-grep-language), with no Python or Node runtime in its gate path.
What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not a change to the Python or TypeScript rules. Not autofix: report-only, as the other languages are. Not a dylint compiler plugin as the required engine: ast-grep YAML plus the ast-grep crates is the engine lobaria already runs (lobaria chart/src/ast_grep_gate.rs, lob-979). The duplicate-type check does not flag two types that share only a name when their shapes differ (lobaria's per-module Refused, Carried, Hit and Finding types are distinct types with local meaning).
Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) aspergillus docs/design.md sections 'Level 2', 'Level 3', 'Catalog rules ASP4xx', 'Whole-project CLI tools' (check-duplicates, asp-21d); typescript/ast-grep-rules/*.yml; lobaria chart/src/ast_grep_gate.rs and scripts/gates/core-types-rules/*.yml (ast-grep YAML rules run on ast-grep-core/config/language 0.40.0 from Rust); lobaria integrated a027fb9: 454 pub type declarations carry 384 distinct names, 45 names declared more than once.
What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1

The check reads a whole Cargo workspace and compares functions across the crates of that workspace. It matches the behavior that `aspergillus check-duplicates` gives for Python. See aspergillus docs/design.md section 'Whole-project CLI tools' (check-duplicates, asp-21d). The check prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. A finding in a blocking rule makes the run fail. The check reports only. It does not autofix. A consumer runs the check with cargo. No Python runtime and no Node runtime is in the gate path. The first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates. This work does not change the Python check or the TypeScript rules.
restatement:
Aspergillus today gives a duplicate-function check for Python only. The `rust/` tree holds reference configs and holds no executable check. This request adds a duplicate-function check for Rust.

A consumer runs the check with cargo. The check reads a whole Cargo workspace in one run. It parses the Rust functions of every member crate of that workspace. It normalizes each function body in the same manner the Python check normalizes a Python function body: it replaces each identifier with one placeholder, and it replaces each literal with a marker for the type of that literal. It then groups the functions by the normalized body. It reports a group that holds more than one function. A duplicate pair whose two copies sit in two different crates is reported, because the comparison covers the whole workspace and not one crate at a time. The behavior matches what `aspergillus check-duplicates` gives for Python (docs/design.md, section 'Whole-project CLI tools', pebble asp-21d).

The check prints each finding on its own line, in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. A finding under a blocking rule makes the run fail with a non-zero exit status. A run that finds nothing exits with status 0.

The check reports only. It edits no source file and it removes no duplicate function.

Cargo alone runs the check. The gate path holds no Python runtime and no Node runtime. The first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates, so the check must read a multi-crate workspace.

This work adds a new surface. It does not change the Python check in `python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py`. It does not change the TypeScript rules in `typescript/rules/`.

One note on a tension in the request. The Python check prints a grouped report, not `path:line: ASPnnn` lines. The request states the `path:line: ASPnnn` format for the Rust check in plain words. This spec therefore reads the parity statement as parity of DETECTION — which pairs of functions count as duplicates. It reads the format statement as the governing rule for what the check prints.

restatement_clauses.text: A consumer runs the duplicate-function check with cargo. The check reports two Rust functions whose normalized bodies are identical. It reports nothing when no two function bodies are identical.
The check reads a whole Cargo workspace in one run. It reports a duplicate pair whose two copies sit in two different member crates of that workspace.

The check matches the detection behavior of `aspergillus check-duplicates` for Python. It reports two functions that differ only in identifier names and in literal values of the same type. It does not report two functions whose bodies differ in structure.
The check prints each finding on its own line, in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`, where ASPnnn is a rule code of three digits.
A finding under a blocking rule makes the run fail with a non-zero exit status. A run with no finding exits with status 0.
The check reports only. It leaves every source file byte-identical. It removes no duplicate function.
Cargo alone runs the check. The check reports the duplicate with no python3 and no node on PATH.
This work does not change the Python duplicate check in `python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py`.
This work does not change the TypeScript rules in `typescript/rules/`.

goal: Give aspergillus a cargo-run duplicate-function check that reports identical normalized Rust function bodies across a whole Cargo workspace.
acceptance_criteria: A person makes a throwaway Rust project that holds two functions with the same body. Cargo runs the check. The check names that pair. The same person makes a second project whose two functions do different work. The check names no pair there.

A person makes a throwaway Cargo workspace of three member crates. The same function body sits in the first crate and in the third crate. One run of the check at the top of the workspace names both copies, and the two copies belong to two different crates.

A person puts two pairs of functions in a throwaway workspace. The first pair does the same work, but the two copies use different variable names and different number values. The second pair does genuinely different work. The check names the first pair and it does not name the second pair.

A person runs the check over a throwaway workspace that holds a duplicate. Every printed line that names a Rust file reads as a file path, then a colon, then a line number, then a colon, then a space, then a rule code of the form ASP and three digits.
A person runs the check over a throwaway workspace that holds a duplicate under a blocking rule. The run fails. The same person runs the check over a workspace with no duplicate. That run succeeds.

A person records the contents of every Rust file in a throwaway workspace that holds a duplicate. The check runs. Afterwards no file differs from its recorded contents, and both copies of the duplicated function are still there.
A person hides python3 and node so that neither program can start. Cargo then runs the check over a throwaway workspace that holds a duplicate. The check still names the duplicate.
The Python duplicate-finding file still names all five of its public functions, so this work left the Python check in place.
Both TypeScript rule files still name the asp202-min-assertions rule, so this work left the TypeScript rules in place.
